label_review: session 2 (H-07), 2026-10-29 to 2026-10-30: R1-R40 checked by an AI and adopted by the product owner's ruling of 2026-10-30; 23 yes, 8 '?' (every required level) and 9 no (every anchor set, and the NMC check), so the reference stays proposed
notes: Written by an agent (Task 9) for the England option pack 0.1.0, and carried unchanged to the reviewed pack 0.2.0 (Task 7c): proposed rubrics, ESCO crosswalks and gate types. Provisional - no specialist review of the parts session 2 did not accept.

Session 2 (R1-R40): yes to the four ESCO occupation crosswalks (R1-R4), every observable task (R5, R9, R13, R17, R21, R25, R29, R33), every ESCO skill crosswalk (R8, R12, R16, R20, R24, R28, R32, R36), both gate types (R37, R39) and the right-to-work check (R40). '?' to every proposed required level 2 (R6, R10, R14, R18, R22, R26, R30, R34): the postings do not establish that entry threshold. No to every anchor set (R7, R11, R15, R19, R23, R27, R31, R35): 'No evidence yet' must stay unknown, never level 0. No to the NMC check (R38): a matching PIN alone is not enough; check the registration's status, its register entry and any restrictions. The no and '?' answers change the capability model's own rules, so nothing here changes until that review (carried to Task 10); a rubric that changes is a new rubric version.

Levels follow spec section 8: 0 no evidence of performance; 1 performs with guidance; 2 independently handles routine tasks; 3 handles complex or non-routine tasks; 4 designs or leads and can justify trade-offs. Unknown is not a level, and levels are never added together.
Required levels are proposals for entry-level roles in the pack's postings; the postings state no behaviourally anchored level.
ESCO crosswalks name one ESCO skill per row, chosen for its description; each named skill is an essential relation of the target's crosswalked occupation in ESCO v1.2.1.

targets.note: ESCO holds no label 'data quality analyst'; its data quality specialists review data for accuracy and integrity.
ESCO lists 'IT support technician' as an alternative label of this occupation.
ESCO lists 'adult nurse' as an alternative label and records the occupation as regulated.
ESCO holds no label 'bookkeeping assistant'; its bookkeepers record day-to-day transactions in the ledgers and balance them.

rubrics.observable_task: Write and check a SQL query that joins two tables to answer a question about the data.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of writing a query against a database.
anchors.1: Writes a simple query with a filter when given an example or step-by-step help.
anchors.2: Independently joins two tables, explains how missing keys change the row count and checks the result.
anchors.3: Writes multi-step queries (grouping, subqueries or window functions) on unfamiliar tables and finds why a result looks wrong.
anchors.4: Designs the querying approach for others, reviews their queries and justifies trade-offs between correctness, clarity and speed.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: the tables joined, the question answered and how the result was checked
A short work sample: join two given tables and explain the row count

rubrics.observable_task: Find a data quality problem (missing, duplicated or inconsistent values), trace its cause and fix or report it.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of checking data for quality problems.
anchors.1: Spots an obvious problem, such as a blank or a duplicate, when shown what to look for.
anchors.2: Independently checks a dataset for missing, duplicated and inconsistent values, traces a problem to its source and records the fix.
anchors.3: Investigates problems that cross systems or have no obvious cause, and designs checks that stop them recurring.
anchors.4: Sets data quality rules and processes for a team and justifies which problems to fix first.

acceptable_proof: A recent example of a data problem found, its cause and what was done about it
A short work sample: list the quality problems in a small given table

rubrics.observable_task: Explain what an analysis found, and how far it can be trusted, to a colleague without a technical background.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of explaining findings to others.
anchors.1: Shares results for others to interpret, or explains them with help.
anchors.2: Independently explains a finding and its limits in plain words to a non-technical colleague and checks they understood it.
anchors.3: Handles a disagreement or a difficult message about the data, adapting the explanation to different audiences.
anchors.4: Leads how findings are reported across a team and justifies what to leave out and why.

acceptable_proof: A structured account of explaining a result, or of resolving a disagreement about it
Optionally, a short note or slide written for a non-technical reader

rubrics.observable_task: Find the cause of a fault on a computer, printer or other device and fix it, or escalate it with a clear record.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of diagnosing a device fault.
anchors.1: Fixes a common fault by following a set checklist, with help.
anchors.2: Independently diagnoses common hardware faults and fixes them, or escalates with a clear record of what was tried.
anchors.3: Diagnoses intermittent or unusual faults across several devices or components.
anchors.4: Designs the fault-finding procedures others use and justifies repair-or-replace decisions.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: the fault, how it was diagnosed and how it was resolved
A short work sample: talk through diagnosing a described fault

rubrics.observable_task: Resolve a user's Windows or Microsoft 365 problem (sign-in, mail, files or settings) and explain the fix to them.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of supporting someone else's computer use.
anchors.1: Resolves a familiar problem for a user by following a guide, with help.
anchors.2: Independently resolves common Windows and Microsoft 365 problems for users and explains the fix in plain words.
anchors.3: Resolves unfamiliar or account-wide problems (permissions, device management or licensing) and documents them for others.
anchors.4: Designs how user support is given for a team and justifies its standards and trade-offs.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: the user's problem, what was done and how the user was told
A short work sample: talk through resolving a described sign-in or mail problem

rubrics.observable_task: Log, prioritise, update and close incidents and requests in a service desk tool.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of using a ticketing or service desk tool.
anchors.1: Logs a ticket when shown how, with help to choose its category and priority.
anchors.2: Independently logs, prioritises, updates and closes incidents and requests, keeping the record clear for the next person.
anchors.3: Handles escalations and major incidents, and spots patterns across tickets that point to an underlying problem.
anchors.4: Designs the service desk's processes (for example along ITIL lines) and justifies their priorities and targets.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: an incident logged, prioritised and closed, and the tool used
A short work sample: prioritise and write up three described requests

rubrics.observable_task: Reconcile a bank, supplier or customer account against its statement and resolve the differences.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of reconciling an account.
anchors.1: Matches transactions to a statement when shown how, with help to explain differences.
anchors.2: Independently reconciles a bank or ledger account to its statement, finds the differences and records how each was resolved.
anchors.3: Reconciles accounts with unusual or long-standing differences and corrects the errors behind them.
anchors.4: Designs reconciliation routines and controls for others and justifies them.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: the account reconciled, the differences found and how they were resolved
A short work sample: reconcile a small given statement to a ledger

rubrics.observable_task: Record purchase and sales transactions in the ledgers accurately and keep them up to date.

anchors.0: No evidence yet of keeping ledger or transaction records.
anchors.1: Enters transactions into a ledger or accounting system when shown how, with checking.
anchors.2: Independently records purchase and sales transactions accurately and keeps the ledgers up to date.
anchors.3: Handles non-routine entries (credit notes, accruals or corrections) and keeps the ledgers consistent with each other.
anchors.4: Designs how records are kept for others and justifies its controls.

acceptable_proof: A recent example: the ledgers kept, the system used and how accuracy was checked
A short work sample: post a few given transactions to the right ledgers
